answer:
That name is a genealogy: each layer reads backwards as "this face came from that one". Reading [why](lab:face?name=shell%2Finner%5Bbody%2Fside%5Bbase.outline.bottom%5D%5D) confirms the chain:

1. **`base.outline.bottom`** — the sketch `base` ([script.js:19](lab:open?file=script.js&line=19)) draws a rect called `outline`; `.bottom` is that rect's bottom side entity.
2. **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the extrude `body` sweeps the sketch profile up by `h`. The side wall generated from the bottom segment is named `body/side[base.outline.bottom]`: feature `body`, role `side`, and in brackets the sketch entity it was swept from. So a face's name records the sketch edge that created it — that's why it survives param changes.
3. **`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the shell `shell` (line 21) offsets the body's faces inward by `wall`. The inner face produced by offsetting that particular side wall keeps its ancestry: feature `shell`, role `inner`, bracketed source = the face it came from.

So the whole name answers "which wall of the box is this?" — the inner surface of the wall that grew from the bottom edge of the sketch rectangle. If you later fillet the vertical edges, the wall splits into `…#a`/`…#b` but keeps the same root name; a selector like `j.feat('shell').faces()` or `j.sel.names('faces', ['shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]'])` still finds it. The nested brackets are why genealogy names are best written inside selectors or copied verbatim, not retyped by hand.

The count, solver-style: entities are 4 lines ($l_1..l_4$) plus 2 circles ($h_1, h_2$). Each line has 4 DOF, each circle 3 DOF, so **22 entity DOF**. The constraint Jacobian has **rank 21**:

- 4 coincidences closing the rectangle: −8
- `fix(l1.start)`: −2
- `horizontal(l1)`, `horizontal(l3)`, `vertical(l2)`, `vertical(l4)`: −4

answer:
**On its side** — with the 12 mm extrusion direction (the clip's width, along Y) flat on the bed, so each layer is a copy of the whole side profile. The auto orientation already picked exactly this: direction −Y, **0 mm³ support, 240 mm² bed contact, 12 mm tall, 60 layers** at 0.2 mm ([open the print](lab:show?view=ir)).

Why it's the right way round:

- **Layer lines run along the jaw and the spine, not across them.** The clip works by the jaws bending open as they push onto the 18 mm desk. Printed on its side, those jaws are continuous perimeters in each layer, so the flex lives along a layer, not between them. Printed upright (profile standing on end), the bending happens across 60 stacked layers — the classic print-in-place weak spot — and the grip bumps would stair-step.
- **Nothing to support.** The whole outline is a closed profile; every "overhang" is just the next layer being the same shape shifted slightly, and the lead-ins (the 1 mm ramps at the jaw tips) arrive gradually. The compiler found `overhangArea: 0`.
- **Big, stable bed contact.** The 35 × 12 mm side face is the largest flat face on the part (240 mm²), so no brim is needed and there's no risk of the part tipping.

One thing worth keeping an eye on: at 12 mm of width, the first layer is only 12 mm deep against the bed — fine for PETG with a clean plate, and the job already slices clean (12.1 min, 1.09 m of filament). If you ever reprint a very tall `desk` (say 30–40 mm), the same side-down orientation stays correct; the profile grows along the jaw direction, not the layer stack.

answer:
**Done:** I read the preset, ran the interference pass, and found the answer in the program's decisions rather than in a metric.

**The number:** the interference check (trace pass `interference`, level L5: 0 exact, 3 mesh, 0 box-separated pairs) reports for **pinion–wheel ≈ 0.203 mm** — that's the smallest gap between the pinion's and the wheel's teeth in the default pose (pinion at 0°, wheel at its 5° half-tooth offset). For comparison, base–pinion and base–wheel each come out at ≈ 0.200 mm, which is the spacer stack the script builds in (0.6 mm spacer minus the port's 0.2 mm offset, plus fit-class clearance).

**Caveats I checked and can state plainly:**
- The decision note says these are **display-mesh distances** ("minimum distance between components (display meshes; `{ exact: true }` for the B-rep distance)"). The meshes were deflected 0.057–0.108 mm, so 0.203 mm is approximate, and given the deflection is of that order the true B-rep gap could differ by a tenth of a millimetre.
- 0.203 mm is consistent with the design intent: `j.inspect.gearMesh` reports **backlash 0.4 mm** (total, i.e. split across both flanks, so ~0.2 mm per flank in the engaged pose), and contact ratio 1.611.

**Unfinished:** I did not run the `{ exact: true }` variant to get the exact B-rep minimum distance — I couldn't reach it through the sandbox program's API in the calls I had, and the mesh-based 0.203 mm is what the interference check in the workbench reports. If you want the exact figure, the one-liner is `j.inspect.distance(pinionSel, wheelSel, { exact: true })` on the compiled assembly; I can also sweep the wheel's joint angle through a full revolution to find the pose with the true minimum tooth gap, since 0.203 mm is only the value at the 5° starting pose.

answer:
One full turn moves the rack **113.10 mm** — the pitch circumference of the pinion.

The pinion is `j.lib.gear.spur({ module: mm(2), teeth: 18 })` ([script.js:7](lab:open?file=script.js&line=7)), so its pitch radius is $r = m z / 2 = 2 \times 18 / 2 = 18$ mm, and per the coupling rule travel = $r\,\theta$ with $\theta = 2\pi$ rad:

$$\text{travel} = \pi \, m \, z = \pi \times 2 \times 18 = 113.10 \text{ mm}$$

That matches `j.inspect.gearMesh(pinion, rack)` on the pitch-line distance of 18 mm ([script.js:24](lab:open?file=script.js&line=24)) and the note in [notes.md:11](lab:open?file=notes.md&line=11). Sanity check with the coupling rule: the notes' "move the rack 1.5708 mm" nudge corresponds to $\theta = 1.5708/18$ rad = 5°, a quarter of a tooth pitch ($\pi m = 6.283$ mm per tooth, so 113.10/18 ≈ 6.28 mm per tooth).

answer:
The hinge uses the **`printInPlace` fit class, 0.4 mm per side**. In [script.js:15](lab:open?file=script.js&line=15) it's passed as `clearance: 'printInPlace'`, and the comment at line 12 does the arithmetic that flows from it: $R = d/2 + c + \text{wall} = 1.5 + 0.4 + 1.6 = 3.5$ mm knuckle radius, and the standoff `off = R + c = 3.9` mm. The resolved parameter lives as `gap.printInPlace = 0.4 mm`, and you can see the resolved value with [param](lab:param?name=gap.printInPlace).

**Calibration: no.** The provenance on every gap parameter reads *default fit classes (uncalibrated)* — these are the library defaults (press 0.05 → printInPlace 0.4 mm), not numbers measured on your printer. There's no `fit.uncalibrated` diagnostic visible in the program right now (the hinge suppresses it by declaring the class explicitly), but the source of truth is still the textbook default.

Two ways to firm it up:

1. **Print a coupon and calibrate.** `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole', … })` makes a graded test part; measuring which steps turn freely gives you rows for `j.fit.calibrate(rows)`, which fits `actual = a·nominal + b` and derives your printer's classes. Then `j.fit.profile('my-printer', { classes: { printInPlace: … } })` in the script replaces the defaults with provenance *calibrated*.
2. **Tune the single number.** If you already know your printer needs more or less room, I can override just this class — e.g. `j.fit.profile('mk4-petg', { classes: { printInPlace: mm(0.45) } })` — but that's a guess until you measure.

Note the fit-aware modelling behind it: the Ø3 mm pin is actually modelled at $3 - 2 \times 0.4 = 2.2$ mm diameter and the bores enlarged, so the 0.4 mm isn't just a gap between existing surfaces — it changes the geometry. If you calibrate, that's what gets recomputed. Want me to add the coupon as a separate printable or wire in a calibrated profile?

answer:
That view shows the print orientation (lying on its side), not the profile. Let me look at the outline itself:

The front view shows the whole story. The outline is a **C-shaped clip**: a flat vertical spine on the left, with two jaws reaching right that wrap over and under the desk edge, and a hook opening downward for the cable.

Walking the outline top to bottom (as written in the polyline in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=8)):

- **Top jaw (desk + t):** a thin $t = 3$ mm arm reaching `jaw = 15` mm across the desk's top face. Its tip carries a small **grip bump** — a 2 mm-long ramp down to the desk face, pinching by `grip = 0.6 mm` with a 1 mm lead-in so the clip can be pushed on rather than needing force at a square corner. Your fit rule (0.4–0.8 mm) sits right in the middle at 0.6.
- **Spine (−t):** the vertical back wall, 3 mm thick, standing `desk + 2·t + cable = 35` mm tall — the full height of the part. It's the only place the two jaws are joined, so it carries all the spring flexion when the clip snaps on.
- **Bottom hook and cable channel:** below the spine, the outline folds into a downward-opening channel about 8 mm wide and ~5 mm tall, sized by the `cable` param. Cables hang in this pocket under the desk instead of dangling off the edge; the inner lip steps (`cable + t`, then the `−t − cable/2` ledge) keeps the channel from being a plain slot — it holds the cable's belly while the mouth narrows to $t + cable/2$.
- **Bottom jaw (−t):** mirrors the top jaw under the desk, again `jaw = 15` mm long, with the same grip bump and lead-in at its tip. Together the two bumps pinch the 18 mm board by $2 \times 0.6$ mm total, which is what holds the clip on by friction.

So: one closed C, four expressions (`desk`, `t`, `jaw`, `grip`, `cable`) place every corner — change `desk` to a measured 19 mm and both jaws and the spine height follow, walls never thinner than $t$. Printed on its side, the layer lines run along the jaws and spine, exactly where the clip flexes.

answer:
I'll look at the actual script and the compiled face names before explaining.



## The name is a genealogy, read right to left

`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]` is three links of provenance, each level naming the thing that *made* the face:

- **`base.outline.bottom`** — the sketch entity. [script.js:22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22) calls `.rect('outline', 'w', 'd', { center: true, r: 'r' })`, which mints sides `outline.bottom right top left`, corners `outline.br tr tl bl`, and an `outline.center` construction point. `bottom` is the straight side at $y=-d/2=-20$; the $r=3$ rounds are *separate* arc entities (`outline.br` …), so `bottom` is only the straight run.
- **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the extrude at [script.js:20](lab:open?file=script.js&line=20) sweeps that profile along $+Z$ for `'h'`, giving one side face per profile segment. Role `side`, and the bracket is the source segment that was swept — `body/start` and `body/end` are the two caps, which have no source segment.
- **`shell/inner[…]`** — the shell at [script.js:25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25) opens `j.feat('body').endFace()` (the $z=30$ cap, `body/end`) and offsets the remaining material inward by `wall`. Each face it generates gets role `inner`, and the bracket records the *input face it was offset from*: the outer bottom wall → an inner bottom wall; `body/start` → `shell/inner[body/start]`, the internal floor at $z=2$.

So brackets are "derived from", never a boolean. Nothing in the script spells this name: it is computed, and it survives edits because each link names a semantic source rather than an ID or index. Change `wall` and the name is unchanged (only the geometry moves); rename the rect (`'outline'` → `'outline2'`) or its line, and every name downstream renames with it, which is what makes it safe to select on.

Concretely, that face is the flat inner bottom wall: [select](lab:face?name=shell/inner%5Bbody/side%5Bbase.outline.bottom%5D%5D) gives a plane at centre $(0,-18,16)$ with normal $+Y$, area $1512 = 54 \times 28\ \text{mm}^2$ — the 54 mm straight run (56 mm cavity less the two $r=1$ inner corner arcs, which are the `%cylinder` faces `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.br]]`) by the 28 mm from floor $z=2$ to rim $z=30$. That arithmetic is the cross-check that the bracket chain really points at the bottom wall and not the floor.

One caveat to expect: if a later feature splits this face (a hole cut through the wall), the two halves keep the name with a `#a` / `#b` suffix, so a selector written against the unsuffixed name would go stale — the reason to prefer intent selectors like `j.feat('shell').faces('<Y')` or `.sideFace(...)` when the shape is still moving.

## It fails — and it fails at exactly 3 mm

`check(null, { override: { wall: '3 mm' } })` compiles the open files in the sandbox with only the wall overridden; nothing was written and the Params view was not touched.

```
error  feature.failed  at: shell  line 25
shell of body1 by 3 mm failed (OpenCascade could not offset the faces)
fix: reduce the thickness or remove small fillets first
```

The reason is the sketch: the outline is a 60 × 40 rectangle with corner radius `r = 3 mm` ([script.js:22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22)), and the shell at [line 25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25) offsets **inward**. The inner corners of the cavity get radius $r_{\text{in}} = r - t$, so at $t = 3$ mm the inner corner radius is exactly zero — the offset surface collapses into a cusp and the kernel refuses. Scanning the wall in steps of 0.05 mm puts the boundary right at the corner radius: 2.98 mm and 2.99 mm compile, 3.00 mm fails. Every value above 3 mm up to the slider's 5 mm maximum also fails (with `shell failed` rather than the offset message). So the `wall` slider's exposed range `[0.8, 5] mm` at [line 17](lab:open?file=script.js&line=17) can drive the part into a broken state.

Where it does work, the numbers are consistent with a cavity $54 \times 34 \times 27$ mm (3 mm floor, sides and 0.99 mm inner corners), i.e. exact B-rep volumes from `check()`: wall 2 mm → 15 344 mm³ / 19.03 g (the open program's value, so the override reproduces it), 2.5 mm → ~18.9 cm³, 2.99 mm → 22 130 mm³. Had 3 mm been acceptably offset, the ideal solid would be ~22 196 mm³ ($2392.3\ \mathrm{mm}^2 \times 30 - 1836 \times 27$) — about 27.5 g, i.e. 44 % more plastic than the 2 mm box.

Two ways out, both checkable without editing: raise the corner radius (`r = 4 mm` at wall 3 mm compiles, 22 039 mm³ / 27.33 g), or tie it to the wall. I verified the latter as a script variant — replacing line 8's `r: mm(3)` with `r: 'wall + 1 mm'` keeps a constant 1 mm inner corner radius: 2 mm → 15 344 mm³ (identical to today), 3 mm → 22 039 mm³ / 27.33 g, 5 mm → 33 594 mm³ / 41.66 g, all compiling. If you want it, that is a one-line [edit](lab:open?file=script.js&line=8); say the word and I'll apply it.

I added the fillet, but 25 mm does not fit this footprint — so I used the largest radius the kernel accepts and left the radius as a param so you can change it.

**Why 25 fails.** Two adjacent vertical fillets eat $2r$ out of the 40 mm depth, so $r \le 20$; the kernel's exact limit at `d = 40` is **19.92 mm** (`fillet.tooLarge: r = 25 mm is too large for 4 edges of body1; the largest that works is about 19.922 mm`). Even at `d = 50` a 25 mm fillet is refused (max 24.8 mm); it needs `d ≥ 50.6 mm`.

**What I changed** in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=8): the sketch rectangle is now sharp (`r: 'r'` dropped from `.rect('outline', …)`), the `r` param became the corner radius with a new rolling-ball fillet before the shell, so the wall follows the round:

```js
.fillet(j.feat('body').sideFaces().edges('|Z'), 'r', { id: 'round' })   // line 25
.shell(j.feat('body').endFace(), 'wall', { direction: 'in', id: 'shell' })
```

At `r = 19.9 mm` it compiles clean: 3 features, 19 faces, volume **13 055.0 mm³**, mass 16.19 g, DOF 0, no warnings. The four outer corner faces are exact cylinders Ø39.8 (`round/face[body/side[base.outline.bottom] ∩ body/side[base.outline.left]]` etc.) and the four inner ones Ø35.8 — the 2 mm wall survives the bend. The [axo view](lab:view?name=axo) shows the near-stadium shape, with 60 × 40 × 30 bbox unchanged.

To get a true 25 mm: widen the box first, e.g. [param d = 51 mm](lab:param?name=d&value=51 mm), then set [param r = 25 mm](lab:param?name=r&value=25 mm) — I checked that pair and it compiles (volume 14 723.6 mm³). answer:
It prints **standing on its side profile** — build direction `−Y`, i.e. the 12 mm extrusion axis straight up.

The compiler picked it itself; I didn't announce a direction in the script. `program.print()` reports `dir: "-Y", supportVolume: 0, bedContact: 240.4 mm², height: 12 mm, overhangArea: 0`, and `program.decisions()` shows the orient decision with its alternatives. The rule is lexicographic: least support first, then the most bed contact, then the least height. Two candidates tie on support (0 mm³) — `−Y` and `+Y`, which are the same pose mirrored — and both give exactly the profile's own area on the bed: 240.4 mm², which is the area of [body/start](lab:face?name=body/start) and [body/end](lab:face?name=body/end), the two flat XZ faces of the extrude. So the eighteen-point outline in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=7) *is* the first layer, and the height is just `w` = 12 mm (60 layers at 0.2 mm). The tie between `−Y` and `+Y` is broken by list order; either gives the identical print, so nothing hinges on it.

The orientations it rejected say why the choice matters. Standing it as the desk sees it (`+Z` up, the jaws opening upward) wants 1510 mm³ of support and 168 mm² of bed contact at 35 mm tall; `−Z` is 1451 mm³ of support; `+X` supports only 134 mm³ but spends 18 mm of height. Those are all the "natural" poses, and all of them hold the jaw tips and the hook up in the air.

The reason the flat pose is also the *right* pose for this part is the flex. The jaws are cantilevers that open ~0.6 mm per side in the XZ plane, so the bending axis is Y. Lying the profile on the bed stacks the layers perpendicular to Y, which puts every layer interface in-plane with the bending stress: no layer line runs across a jaw, so squeezing the clip on pulls the layers along their strong direction instead of peeling them off each other. It's also why [notes.md](lab:open?file=notes.md&line=23) picks PETG over PLA, which would rather snap than splay. And with zero overhang area, the lead-ins and grip bumps in the outline come out as drawn with no supports to clean up out of the 8 mm channel.

The numbers I'm quoting: geometry is exact B-rep (volume 2,884.8 mm³, mass 3.66 g, height 12 mm); support volume, bed contact and the 12.1 min print time are the slicer's approximate model.

I'll look at the hinge definition and the fit/clearance in the compiled program.



**The clearance.** The hinge is declared at [script.js:15–16](lab:open?file=script.js&line=15) with `clearance: 'printInPlace'`, i.e. the print-in-place fit class. Resolved in the open program that is `gap.printInPlace = 0.4 mm` **per side**. It shows up twice in the geometry:

- radially, between pin and knuckle bore — the bore faces `hinge/bore2` and `hinge/bore4` come out at radius **1.9 mm** against a pin of radius **1.5 mm** (Ø3.8 bore on a Ø3.0 pin), so 0.4 mm on each side;
- axially, between adjacent knuckles, where the same 0.4 mm `c` also sets the knuckle length [script.js:13](lab:open?file=script.js&line=13) and the back-wall standoff `off = R + c` [script.js:12](lab:open?file=script.js&line=12), so neighbouring knuckles don't rub and each half's wall clears the other's knuckles.

`.printInPlace(['base','lid'], { clearance: mm(c), pose: { hinge: deg(0) } })` at [script.js:62](lab:open?file=script.js&line=62) checks those gaps in the print pose; the run currently reports no diagnostics.

**Is it calibrated?** No. Every gap param carries the provenance `default fit classes (uncalibrated)` — the `gap.*` params ([params view](lab:show?params)) are the library defaults, and a grep of the script for `.fit(...)` / `j.fit.profile(...)` finds nothing, so no `j.fit.profile('mk4-petg', …)` is applied. The 0.4 mm is a nominal starting value, not measured on your printer.

To calibrate, you'd print the coupon ([C-04 Print-in-place clearance](lab:preset/C-04), or `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole', steps: 10 })`), feed the results to `j.fit.calibrate(...)` to get a `j.fit.profile(...)`, and attach it with `.fit(profile)` on the part that builds the hinge (the `j.print` job's part at [script.js:68](lab:open?file=script.js&line=68)). Until then, if you know your printer needs a different gap, the honest fix is either that profile or overriding `gap.printInPlace` — but note the `c = 0.4` literal at [script.js:12](lab:open?file=script.js&line=12) is a separate hand-entered number, so it must be moved in step with the fit class or the axial gap will disagree with the radial one.

**What broke.** `script.js` had `l1` dimensioned twice: [line 20](lab:open?file=script.js&line=20) `.dim('l1', 'w')` (w = 80 mm) and [line 22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22) `.dim('l1', 90)`. **DOF before and after**, in solver terms:
- *Before:* 6 entities, 17 constraints. DOF $= \Sigma\,\text{entity DOF} - \operatorname{rank}J$. With the duplicate length dim the system is *inconsistent* — the two length rows are linearly dependent but agree on nothing, so no rank of $J$ yields a solution: `sketch.overConstrained`, no compile.
- *After:* 6 entities, 16 constraints, $\operatorname{rank}J$ is one short of the entity DOF, giving **dof = 1**. On the solver: each constraint or dimension adds a row to $J$; `rank J` is how many independent rows it actually bought. A duplicate dimension adds a row that is a multiple of an existing one — it raises neither rank nor solvability, which is why the fix is to *drop* the extra row rather than change a value. Had you wanted a reference measurement instead, the accepted fix is to make it `driven: true` so it reports 80 mm without entering the solve.

The outline lies on XZ in sketch `side` ([script.js:6](lab:open?file=script.js&line=6)), with $x$ running into the desk and $z$ up; the profile is 18 × 35 mm and is extruded $w = 12$ mm. **Walking the outline in polyline order** ([script.js:7](lab:open?file=script.js&line=7)):

- **Top jaw outer face**, line 8: $z = desk + t = 21$, from $x=15$ back to $x=-3$ — the whole jaw plus the spine cap; the face you see from above the desk, and the arm that flexes.
- **Spine outer face**, line 10: $x = -t = -3$, from $z=21$ down to $-2t-cable = -14$ — 35 mm, the back of the clip and its spring.
- **Hook floor**, line 12: $z=-14$, $x=-3 \to cable+t = 11$ — the bottom of the cable trough.
- **Lip**, lines 13–15: outer face at $x = cable+t = 11$ up to $z = -t-cable/2 = -7$, a 3 mm top at $z=-7$ back to $x = cable = 8$, then down its inner face to $z = -t-cable = -11$. This little rib (3 wide × 4 tall) is what keeps a cable from falling out of the trough.
- **Channel floor and back**, lines 16–17: $z=-11$ from $x=8$ to $0$, then up the spine's inner face to $z=-t=-3$ — so the trough is exactly $cable \times cable/2$, i.e. 8 × 4 mm, open at the top under the bottom jaw.
- **Bottom jaw underside**, line 18: $z = -t = -3$, $x=0 \to jaw = 15$ — 3 mm below the board.
- **Bottom jaw tip and grip**, lines 19–22: the end face at $x=15$ rises only 2 mm ($z=-3 \to -1$), then a **lead‑in ramp** to the grip bump at $(13,\ 0.6)$ and back to the board's underside at $(11,\ 0)$. So the jaw is flush from $x=0$ to 11, contacts only at the bump, and the bump bites $grip = 0.6$ mm into the board.
- **The mouth**, lines 23–24: back along the board's underside $z=0$ from $x=11$ to $x=0$, then up the desk edge $x=0$ to $z = desk = 18$. That 15 × 18 slot is the board itself — the mouth is the measured thickness with no slop on the edge.
- **Top jaw inner face**, lines 25–27: the mirror of the bottom — flush at $z=18$ for 11 mm, a $grip = 0.6$ mm dip to $(13,\ 17.4)$, then the lead‑in flare out to the tip at $(15,\ 19)$, thinning the jaw to 2 mm there.

Two things the outline is doing deliberately: every jaw has a ramp at its tip (the "no jaw without a lead‑in" rule) so the clip slides on rather than stabbing the board, and the thinnest walls are the 2 mm jaw tips — the spine, jaws and lip are all $t = 3$ mm, so nothing is under 2 mm.
